title: Fellowship (Acts 2:42)
hookLine: the first believers devoted themselves to teaching, fellowship, bread and prayers
carry: you weren't meant to do it alone

cards: Jerusalem, a few weeks after Easter. Something has happened at Pentecost, and suddenly there are thousands of new believers where there were about a hundred and twenty. No church buildings.
No clergy training. No plan. So what do they do, day to day?
The book of Acts gives a snapshot, and it's surprisingly ordinary. They listen to the apostles teach. They eat together in each other's homes.
They pray. They share what they have, so nobody goes without. It reads less like the founding of a religion than a very large family learning to live together.

teach.b: Koinonia comes from koinos: common, shared, what belongs to everyone. Koinonia is having something in common: partnership, participation, sharing.
English usually says fellowship, which is fine, but it's thicker than coffee after church.
The verse, in the King James Bible: "And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers."
Teaching, fellowship, bread, prayers. Churches still use that verse as a checklist.

teach.h: A MEAL, MONEY, THE CUP, SUFFERING.
teach.b: Elsewhere in the New Testament, Paul uses koinonia for money: a collection the churches took up for poor believers in Jerusalem.

He uses it for the bread and cup: "The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ?" That word communion is koinonia. And he uses it for sharing in someone's suffering.
One word covers a meal, a bank transfer, the Lord's Supper and a hard season.
That tells you what the first Christians thought church was: not an event you attend, but a life you share. Acts says they ate their meals with gladness.

teach.h: IT IS NOT GOOD THAT THE MAN SHOULD BE ALONE.
teach.b: Underneath it all sits a line from the very start of Genesis: "It is not good that the man should be alone." Some churches keep a meal after every service.

Orthodox and Catholic Christians speak of the whole church, living and dead, sharing one communion. Many Protestants meet in homes midweek. Different forms, one conviction: faith was never meant to be carried solo.

how: Many churches keep fellowship through shared meals, coffee after services, home groups and collections for people in need, and many Christians take Acts 2:42 as a picture of what church life should include.

games.q: you're one of thousands of new believers in Jerusalem. there are no buildings, no clergy, no plan. what do you do?
o: wait for leaders to organize something.
listen to the apostles, eat together, pray and share.
games.why: they continued in teaching, fellowship, breaking of bread and prayers, eating together in homes with gladness, sharing so nobody went without.

practice: Picture the last meal you really shared with someone, not just ate near: where you were, what you talked about.
Then let a face come to mind, someone you haven't eaten with in too long, a friend, a neighbor, a parent, someone who might be lonelier than they let on, and hold it for a minute.
If you pray, pray for them by name; if you don't, just wish them well.

wordCard.voice: Koinonia. Greek for sharing a common life. Fellowship, communion, partnership: a meal, a purse and a faith held together.

orig.note: Greek: sharing, partnership, communion — from koinos, common.
